They are something in between a crayon and cary-pas and a watercolor pencil. I also tried Himi/ Miya watercolors and liked those much better than other nwer brands I had tried. Their watercolors do use pigment, rather than dye, like the vast majority of inexpensive watercolor paint. The crayons are almost certainly dye based. I did not get the breakup which you see with pigments in their crayons that I did with their watercolors. On the left is a little sample of their crayons. I actually tried to reproduce the doodle I did to test their watercolors. The crayons are on the left and watercolors on the right.The Silkky crayons did blend with water, but it too a lot of water, so much that it bled through (the green spots on the right are bleed through). I was able to smudge/ blend a bit when dry, and the water did smooth it out some, but not to the extent that you get with real watercolor paint.As a crayon it is a joy to use. It really does glide! There was not a sharpener included, though no doubt the could be brought to a point with a knife. That said, they are not precise like watercolor pencils, but like watercolor pencils, do leave a more definite line than you get with watercolor paint. They are waxy, but it is a soft wax, even softer than cray-pas.They are not much like Windson Newton watercolor crayons, which are from their pro line, and densely pigmented. Unfortunately, Windsor Newton has discontinued their crayons, and as far as I know, Himi is the closest available, though, again, the Windor Newton were pigment based and the Himi dye based. The Himi crayons are a lot less expensive, which also makes them easier to play with. That is, they are not so costly that I feel like I can only take them out when I am ready to do some serious work....which is great! It leaves a lot of room for experimentation.They are easy to use, twist out like a lipstick. Unfortunately there is not a huge amount of each color. The staick are around 1/2 inch long each. On the other hand, this is very inexpensive for a set of 36 colors, so replacing the set when one or more is used up is not too costly.Very little of what is on the package is in English, so I can not report on the content (pigment vs. dye e.g.). There are only 2 things in English on the package: 36 colors, and *Not suitable for use by children under 3 years old*. I am a bit confused because the description talks about use as face paint, and children's parties... I had the impression from the description that they were non-toxic, which is why I am puzzled about the warning for children under 3. (It also appears in a graphic on the box).If there is a representative here from Himi, could you please clarify? Why is there a warning that these are not suitable for use by those under 3?Ordered it as a present and got complemets about the colors and comfortability of use.My girl loves it because the color is so vivid, they make her drawings pop. It comes in 36 awesome colors. The crayons are creamy and glide smoothly. It's easy to use even for my toddler. The thick fat pens is easy for him to grip. It really help him to hold pen correctly. These also don't break as easily as the twistable Crayola we used to have. On the downside, they go through a lot each time they color so the set will probably not last long. They do have to wait for at least five minutes after they color. It's a bit wet and will leave marks everywhere if you don't let it dry. That said, they're easy to wash off the hands.My daughter loves these crayons. They are so easy to color with and their pigment is out of this world. They are easy to wipe off if you accidentally get them on the table . They feature a roll-up bottom to bring out more crayons. Way better than a box of crayons.
